clips.title: AWS Lambda explained in 90 seconds | Amazon Web Services
clips.why: AWS's own 90-second summary of what Lambda is and why you would use it.
look: Code that runs in response to events, with no servers to manage.
Paying only for the time the code runs, which suits a job that works a few seconds every 15 minutes.
clips.after: The sweeper is exactly this kind of job: a few seconds of work, four times an hour, with no server of ours to keep alive.

clips.title: AWS Lambda Function Execution and Cold Start
clips.why: What happens in a full cold start and in a partial one, and which part of your code runs when.
look: A full cold start: a fresh environment, the runtime, then your code outside the handler.
A partial cold start, and why reused environments are so much faster.
Compare it with the two REPORT lines in the lab: about 200 ms, then about 6 ms.
clips.after: That is why the sweeper creates its EC2 client outside the handler: warm calls reuse it.

clips.title: AWS Lambda & EventBridge: Mastering Scheduled Tasks (Cron Jobs)
clips.why: Adding an EventBridge schedule as a Lambda trigger, with the schedule syntax explained.
look: Adding a trigger to the function, and choosing EventBridge.
The two kinds of schedule expression: cron(...) and rate(...). Ours is rate(15 minutes).
clips.after: In the platform the same trigger is written in Terraform, and it fires the sweeper every 15 minutes whether or not anything else is running.

practice.q: Complete the schedule expression that fires the sweeper every 15 minutes.
practice.hint: EventBridge has rate(...) and cron(...); the simpler one fits.
practice.why: rate(15 minutes) sends an event every 15 minutes, and the function is the rule's target.

practice.q: Which VM does the sweeper's lease rule terminate?

options.text: Tagged ai-agents:managed=true, with a run ID and a lease 2 hours ahead
options.why: A lease in the future means a live run is still moving it forward.

options.text: No ai-agents:managed tag, with a run ID and a lease that passed
options.why: Without our tag the sweeper never looks at it, and its role could not terminate it.

options.text: Tagged ai-agents:managed=true, with a run ID and a lease that passed
options.why: Ours, claimed, and no one is moving the lease: no live run owns it.

practice.q: Put one sweep in order, from the schedule to the log line.
items: The EventBridge schedule fires and sends an event to the function
On a cold start, Python loads and the EC2 client is created outside the handler
The handler lists the VMs tagged ai-agents:managed=true
It finds a VM with a run ID and a lease in the past
It prints one JSON line and, with dry run off, terminates the VM
practice.why: The cold-start setup happens only on a fresh copy. Every call, warm or cold, lists the VMs again, because nothing from an earlier call can be trusted.

practice.q: Complete the line in act() so a dry run reports the decision without doing anything.
practice.hint: The setting that is on by default.
practice.why: The JSON line is printed every time; the terminate call only happens when dry run is off.

practice.q: A run is waiting on a question, so its VM is parked (stopped). Why doesn't the sweeper terminate it after 15 minutes?

options.text: Because the sweeper skips stopped VMs
options.why: The sweeper does look at stopped VMs; it even has a rule for VMs stopped longer than 72 hours.

options.text: Because a parked VM gets a lease of 73 hours, so its lease is still in the future
options.why: Parking sets the lease far ahead on purpose. If nobody answers for 3 days, the run retires the VM itself, and the sweeper is the backstop.

options.text: Because the orchestrator tells the sweeper which VMs are parked
options.why: The sweeper never talks to the orchestrator. Everything it knows comes from tags.
